bill.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
bill.latestActionText: Became Public Law No: 119-12.

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new content moderation obligations and 48-hour removal requirements on social media platforms and user-generated content websites.
New criminal prohibitions and mandatory restitution provisions would generate litigation and enforcement work related to intimate image publication.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would make it a federal crime to publish intimate images or videos of someone online without their consent, including computer-generated deepfakes, when the publication is intended to cause harm or involves a minor. Social media platforms and similar websites would be required to remove such content within 48 hours after receiving a complaint from the person depicted. Violators would face criminal penalties including prison time, fines, and mandatory restitution to victims.

plain.whoItTouches: Children, and the adults responsible for them. Anyone who uses the internet.

bill.title: HALT Fentanyl Act
bill.latestActionText: Became Public Law No: 119-26.

industries.rationale: The bill changes registration and licensing requirements for pharmaceutical researchers conducting controlled substance research and affects the regulatory classification of chemical substances.
The bill establishes new criminal penalties and quantity thresholds that will affect prosecution and defense of drug trafficking cases.
Universities and research institutions conducting controlled substance research would be subject to the new registration processes and requirements established by the bill.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would permanently classify all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I controlled substances, meaning they would be treated as having high abuse potential and no accepted medical use. It sets the same criminal penalties and quantity thresholds for fentanyl-related substances as currently apply to fentanyl analogues. The bill also creates a streamlined registration process for researchers studying Schedule I substances and relaxes some requirements for research facilities working with controlled substances.

plain.whoItTouches: People caught up in the criminal law, and victims of crime.

bill.title: A joint resolution proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States relating to contributions and expenditures intended to affect elections.
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: Organizations that spend money to influence elections would face new potential restrictions on their expenditures and fundraising.
The amendment would create new constitutional authority to regulate campaign finance, directly affecting election law practice and lobbying activity.
Limits on campaign spending could affect demand for political advertising across broadcast, digital, and print media platforms.
The amendment's authorization to distinguish between natural persons and corporations could affect how financial institutions participate in election-related spending.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution proposes a constitutional amendment that would allow Congress and state governments to set limits on how much money candidates and others can raise and spend to influence elections. It would also permit lawmakers to treat corporations and other legal entities differently from individual people, including by prohibiting those entities from spending money on elections. The amendment would require ratification by three-fourths of the states to take effect.

bill.title: SAFE Drugs Act of 2026
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 524.
subjects: Department of Health and Human Services
Drug safety, medical device, and laboratory regulation

industries.rationale: The bill directly regulates compounding pharmacies and outsourcing facilities, imposing new definitions, frequency limits, reporting requirements, and inspection obligations on drug compounding operations.
Physicians who compound drugs or prescribe compounded medications face new reporting requirements if they exceed the monthly threshold for out-of-state patients.

bill.plainSummary: This bill tightens federal oversight of drug compounding—the practice of mixing or altering medications to meet individual patient needs. It redefines when a compounded drug is considered an "essentially a copy" of an FDA-approved commercial product, raises the monthly limit on such compounding from 4 to 20 prescriptions, and requires annual reporting by physicians and facilities that compound drugs for out-of-state patients more than 20 times per month. Large-scale compounding facilities would face regular inspections and new reporting obligations.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who takes a medicine. People who work in health care, and their patients.

bill.title: A joint resolution terminating the national emergency declared with respect to energy.
bill.latestActionText: Failed of passage in Senate by Yea-Nay Vote. 47 - 51. Record Vote Number: 554.

industries.rationale: The emergency declaration explicitly expedites approvals for oil, gas, and coal development and infrastructure, which this resolution would terminate.
The emergency order covers renewable energy resources and infrastructure, so ending it would affect expedited permitting for solar, wind, and storage projects.
The emergency declaration addresses energy infrastructure and supply adequacy, directly affecting utilities' ability to build transmission and generation facilities under expedited timelines.
The emergency order includes critical minerals and uranium in its definition of energy resources subject to expedited development.
The emergency invokes military construction authority and expedites energy infrastructure projects, affecting contractors who build pipelines, power plants, and related facilities.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would end the national energy emergency that the President declared in January 2025. That emergency declaration directed federal agencies to speed up approvals for energy projects—including oil, gas, coal, renewables, and infrastructure like pipelines—and gave the Defense Department authority to use emergency construction powers to address energy supply vulnerabilities. Terminating the emergency would remove those expedited authorities and return permitting and development processes to their standard procedures.

bill.latestActionText: Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

industries.rationale: The bill's focus on epilepsy treatment, diagnosis, and cure research directly affects pharmaceutical and medical device companies developing epilepsy therapies.
The national plan's coordination of epilepsy care and services would affect hospitals and health systems that diagnose and treat epilepsy patients.

bill.plainSummary: This bill directs the Department of Health and Human Services to create and carry out a national plan to address epilepsy, including prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and research coordination across federal agencies. HHS must establish an advisory council that reports to Congress every two years and must itself submit annual progress reports with recommended actions. These requirements would remain in effect until the end of 2035.

bill.title: Combating Organized Retail Crime Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: The bill directly addresses organized theft targeting retail operations and e-commerce platforms.
The bill explicitly covers theft from interstate and foreign shipments, affecting logistics and shipping companies.
The bill addresses online marketplaces and social media platforms where stolen goods are sold, potentially creating new compliance obligations.
The bill expands money laundering statutes to cover prepaid cards and gift cards, affecting payment processors and card issuers.

bill.plainSummary: This bill expands federal authority to prosecute organized retail theft and supply-chain crime. It allows prosecutors to aggregate the value of stolen goods over a 12-month period to meet felony thresholds, makes these offenses predicate crimes for money laundering charges, and authorizes asset forfeiture. The bill also creates a temporary coordination center within the Department of Homeland Security to help federal agencies work together on these cases.

bill.latestActionText: Motion to discharge Senate Committee on Foreign Relations rejected by Yea-Nay Vote. 47 - 53. Record Vote Number: 46. (consideration: CR S796)

industries.rationale: The resolution would directly affect deployment decisions and operational tempo for defense contractors supporting military operations in or near Iran.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would require the President to withdraw U.S. military forces from any hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress has formally declared war or passed specific authorization for such military action. The measure includes an exception allowing the United States to defend itself and its personnel or facilities abroad if attacked. It does not authorize new military operations but instead seeks to limit existing or future ones that lack explicit congressional approval.

bill.title: Rural Development Hospital Technical Assistance Program Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

industries.rationale: The bill directly targets rural hospitals, providing them with technical assistance, training, and support for operational and financial improvements.
The program explicitly includes increasing telehealth capabilities as a development need, which would affect broadband and telecommunications infrastructure providers serving rural hospitals.
The bill addresses acquiring and upgrading health care information systems including electronic health records, which would involve technology vendors and IT service providers.
The program covers technical assistance for constructing, expanding, and modernizing health care facilities, which would involve construction and engineering firms.

bill.plainSummary: This bill formally establishes a technical assistance program within the Department of Agriculture to help rural hospitals (in areas with 50,000 or fewer residents) improve their operations and finances. The program would provide training and support to help these hospitals modernize facilities, expand telehealth, upgrade information systems, and navigate USDA loan and grant programs. Priority would go to hospitals already participating in certain USDA rural assistance programs, and USDA would report annually to Congress on the program's results.

bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

bill.title: Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Became Public Law No: 119-69.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects dairy producers and processors by expanding the types of milk schools may purchase and serve.
Schools participating in the lunch program face new training requirements and changes to meal planning and procurement rules.
Food service companies and suppliers to school meal programs would adjust product offerings to meet the expanded milk and nondairy beverage options.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would allow schools participating in the National School Lunch Program to offer whole milk and 2% milk to students, in addition to the low-fat and fat-free options currently required. It would expand nondairy milk alternatives, permit parents (not just doctors) to request milk substitutes for students with dietary restrictions, and exclude milk fat from saturated fat limits in school meals. The bill also requires annual food allergy training and certification for school food service staff.

plain.whoItTouches: Parents of young children. People who use food aid.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
